title: Echoes That Stay Warm
summary: In 2034, when lenses write people's replies for them, Leo gets an offer from a company to buy his grandmother's entire way of speaking, enough to pay for her room at a nursing home.
content:
There is a long wooden shelf at the entrance to Echo Station No. 7. On it sit twenty silver dishes the size of coffee saucers, each engraved with a number. People leave their lenses here when they come to work.

I took the lenses out of both eyes and set them on dish No. 14. The two clear lenses clung to the dish like drops of water. The text in front of my eyes went dark. The world grew sharp and smooth, and a little empty.

In 2034, everyone wears lenses. When people don't know what to say, the lenses put a sentence in front of their eyes, and they read it aloud. Declarations of love, apologies, condolences—all of them happen this way. So the city sounds like a letter written by one person. Answers given without lenses have become rare. Echo buys those answers and uses them to teach its models.

When I sit in booth No. 14, a question appears on the screen.

[Question 1,204: A friend who borrowed money and never paid it back has sent you a wedding invitation. Should you go?]

The model writes my answer in advance and keeps it hidden. When I finish speaking, the screen compares the two. The more they overlap, the less I get paid.

Whenever I closed my eyes, I saw the bakery on the island. The oven at four in the morning. Grandma never sold the ends of her loaves. When I came home from school, she would spread butter on a heel and put it in my hand. It was still warm.

“Of course you should go. Have two slices of cake. Deduct the gift from what they owe you.”

[Match 44%]

That meant the model had predicted less than half my answer. The screen in the next booth showed 91%.

Three years ago, my match was 19%. Each year, the number rose like dough.

Echo has a rule. Once a model can predict more than half of someone's answers, the company decides there is nothing left to learn from them. That day, their dish disappears from the shelf. That is the entire dismissal notice.

Before I left work, the branch manager, Mr. Miller, called me into his office. He wears horn-rimmed glasses instead of lenses. He keeps a small cactus on his desk.

“Head office wants to buy your entire way of speaking. Five hundred and twenty thousand dollars. You'll be paid once two hundred expressions pass review.”

Grandma was in a four-bed room at St. Clare Nursing Home. It cost $2,800 a month. A private room was $4,100. Ten years would be $492,000.

“The new version coming out soon will predict more than half your answers. Then, under the rules, dish No. 14 comes off the shelf. They're asking you to sell before that happens.”

Mr. Miller turned his screen toward me. It was a model made from my answers.

[To a son who failed a job interview: Don't comfort him right away. Words are bread, too. Slice them before they cool, and they get squashed.]

It was something Grandma used to say after sitting my impatient younger self down.

“Those aren't my words.”

“We know. ‘My grandma says’ appears more than six hundred times in your answers. We're not allowed to record people over eighty directly. We can only buy words their families remember and pass on. Yours is the only mouth we can listen to.”

The first page of the contract read [Origin: Rosa Marin, born 1945]. I had never seen a piece of paper call Grandma an origin before.

Mr. Miller pushed a pen toward me. He told me to be sure to read Clause 7. It said that even after my dish was removed, I could bring in new words from Grandma and receive $180 for each one.

I went to the nursing home that evening. The old person in the next bed in the four-bed room was coughing. Grandma took my hands first. She said they were cold.

“Leo, do those scales stuck to your eyes listen, too?”

“They only listen. I can't take anything I hear in this room to the company.”

“Then why wear something you can't even take anything with? You're not a fish.”

I laughed while counting the cost of a private room.

“Bring me some bread heels. All they give us here is porridge.”

Grandma had baked bread on the island for fifty years. She never learned to read or write.

“Next time, Grandma.”

I signed on Friday.

The following week, I began reporting to a windowless recording room. For two months, I pulled out every word of Grandma's I could remember. Things she said while kneading dough, at funerals, when I lied. At the hundred and ninety-sixth expression, the well ran dry. I was four short. Grandma only said something new when I fell down. I went to the four-bed room.

“Grandma, I guaranteed a loan for the wrong person. I'm about to lose my house.”

I had never guaranteed a loan. Grandma looked at my ears for a long time.

“Carry your debts on your back. Carry them on your chest, and you won't be able to get up.”

Grandma said it once more. Slowly, as if giving dictation.

Text appeared on my lenses.

[Unregistered expression. Repeat outside the resident's room to submit]

I faced the hallway wall and repeated the sentence. The hallway was quiet.

[Unregistered expression. Submission complete]

When I returned, Grandma put two snack yogurts in my pocket. People in debt needed to eat well, she said. The door to the room had been open the whole time.

I went three more times that week. Each time, I brought a lie. Each time, Grandma said her words twice. Each time, yogurt went into my pocket.

The day I reached two hundred, I had my final review in booth No. 14. The model, having learned all two hundred expressions, had written my answers in advance.

[Match 97%]

On my way out, only a round mark in the dust remained where No. 14 had been on the shelf.

Mr. Miller came to the door and handed me a paper bag. Inside was dish No. 14, with my lenses clinging to it.

“This isn't in the rules. I was going to put it under my cactus, but changed my mind.”

After the new version came out, the city's way of speaking changed a little. That night's weather forecast added a line after the news of rain.

“Today's clouds haven't risen much. The rain will stop before long. Still, take an umbrella. Trust the sky or an oven, and you'll get burned.”

Grandma had never said that. But it sounded like her voice. The next day, I took an umbrella. The rain stopped before long.

A month later, a private room became available. On the day she moved, the afternoon sun lay at the foot of her bed in a square, like a slice of bread.

“No one coughing in here. How will you pay for this room?”

A caregiver wearing lenses rubbed Grandma's back.

“Carry your worries on your back, dear. Carry them on your chest, and you won't be able to get up.”

It was the sentence I had sold in the hallway last month. Grandma put down her spoon and looked at me. I peeled an apple.

After the caregiver left, Grandma took my wrist.

“What happened with that loan you guaranteed?”

“I paid it all off.”

“Did you pay it off by selling my words?”

The knife stopped.

“I said them twice for you. They must have been easy to remember.”

The door to the four-bed room had been open the whole time.

“Grandma, I—”

“Your ears turn red when you lie. They have since you were five.”

Grandma picked up a slice of apple.

“I couldn't send a child who'd brought me a lie away empty-handed. I thought I had nothing to leave behind because I couldn't write. But it turns out I could leave it in your mouth.”

Grandma looked toward the door.

“That young lady said my words. They sounded all right. Bread is baked to be shared.”

Grandma patted the back of my hand.

“But don't give the ends away. The heels belong to the baker.”

I had never heard that before. This time, she said it only once.

[Unregistered expression. Repeat outside the resident's room to submit. Estimated payment $180. Submission deadline 72:00:00]

I went into the hallway. I opened my mouth, then closed it. There was a request I had forgotten after saying “next time” three months ago. I went down the stairs and pushed open the door of the bakery across the street.

“Can I buy just the heels?”

“We don't usually sell those.”

“I know.”

The owner looked at me, then sliced both ends off a fresh loaf and wrapped them in paper. He wouldn't take any money. In the corner of my lenses, the numbers were counting down.

[71:42:10]

Back in the room, I took dish No. 14 out of my bag. I set it on the bedside table, took out my lenses, and placed them on it. The counting numbers went dark. In the sharp, bright room, there was only Grandma's face.

Grandma chewed the heel for a long time.

“Underbaked. Still, it's warm.”

Grandma broke off half and put it in my hand. It was still warm. On the dish on the table, the two lenses were drying like drops of water.
